segments.narration: The most expensive habit I ever quit was answering immediately. It did not look like a habit. It looked like competence — the fast reply, the same-hour turnaround, the reputation for being on top of things.
segments.anchor: The most expensive habit I ever quit was answering immediately. It did not look like a habit. It looked like competence — the fast reply, the same-hour turnaround, the reputation for being on top of things.

segments.narration: I billed it to others as reliability. I experienced it as a low hum of emergency that never once switched off in nine years.
segments.anchor: I billed it to others as reliability. I experienced it as a low hum of emergency that never once switched off in nine years.

segments.narration: The economics of the instant answer are deceptive because the cost is booked to a different account than the benefit. The benefit lands publicly and now: the colleague unblocked, the client soothed, the thread closed.
segments.anchor: The economics of the instant answer are deceptive because the cost is booked to a different account than the benefit. The benefit lands publicly and now: the colleague unblocked, the client soothed, the thread closed.

segments.narration: The cost lands privately and later: the decision made with the first framing that came to mind, the yes that a night's sleep would have made a no, the creeping conviction — mine and everyone else's — that my time was a commons anyone could graze.

segments.narration: Worse, speed compounds into an identity. Answer fast for a year and fast becomes your contract; the grace period others get by default, you now have to negotiate.

segments.narration: I had trained my whole address book, patiently, message by message, to expect of me something I did not want to give.
segments.anchor: I had trained my whole address book, patiently, message by message, to expect of me something I did not want to give.

segments.narration: What broke the habit was not wisdom but an accident: two weeks somewhere with almost no signal. The queue that greeted my return held maybe two hundred items. Perhaps a dozen still needed me.
segments.anchor: What broke the habit was not wisdom but an accident: two weeks somewhere with almost no signal. The queue that greeted my return held maybe two hundred items. Perhaps a dozen still needed me.

segments.narration: The rest had solved themselves, expired, or been quietly handled by people who, given room, turned out to be perfectly capable. Two hundred emergencies; twelve real.
segments.anchor: The rest had solved themselves, expired, or been quietly handled by people who, given room, turned out to be perfectly capable. Two hundred emergencies; twelve real.

segments.narration: That ratio did more for my judgment than any book on attention I ever read, and I had read plenty, always quickly.
segments.anchor: That ratio did more for my judgment than any book on attention I ever read, and I had read plenty, always quickly.

segments.narration: I answer slowly now — not always, not to everything, and to genuine urgency I still move like a fire crew. But the default gap between question and answer has been widened on purpose, and I defend it like a border.
segments.anchor: I answer slowly now — not always, not to everything, and to genuine urgency I still move like a fire crew. But the default gap between question and answer has been widened on purpose, and I defend it like a border.

segments.narration: In that gap, questions ripen or rot, and both outcomes are information. The instant answer treats every question as equally alive. The gap lets the dead ones prove it.

segments.narration: People ask whether the slowness costs me. Of course it costs me. It costs exactly what it looks like: some shine off the reputation, some speed off the wheel.

segments.narration: What I bought with it is the difference between being a switchboard and being a person — and the discovery, humbling on schedule, of how much of my necessity had been decor.
